The earliest lamps were simple-burning animal fat, resin, or plant oils in stone or clay vessels. Ancient Egyptians   
 used rush lights soaked in tallow around 3000 BCE. These rudimentary lamps produced minimal light and substantial     
 smoke but allowed evening work and social gatherings. Oil lamps improved efficiency; the Romans developed             
 sophisticated bronze lamps burning olive oil, establishing a design refined for centuries. Islamic scholars created   
 sophisticated oil lamps used throughout medieval periods.                                                             
                                                                                                                       
 Candles emerged as significant innovations, made from animal tallow or beeswax. Though expensive, beeswax candles     
 burned cleaner and brighter than tallow, becoming luxury items. Candle production became an industrial process by the 
 18th century, though cost remained prohibitive for common people.                                                     
                                                                                                                       
 Gas lighting revolutionized illumination in the 19th century. Coal gas provided bright, reliable light suitable for   
 streets, factories, and homes. Gas lamps proliferated in urban centers, enabling nighttime commerce and reducing      
 crime. However, gas was dangerous-leaks caused explosions and poisoning.                                              
                                                                                                                       
 Thomas Edison's incandescent bulb (1879) transformed civilization. Electric light was safer, cleaner, and ultimately  
 more efficient than gas or candles. Widespread electrification began in wealthy nations, enabling factories to        
 operate continuously and homes to extend productive hours. Electric lighting became a hallmark of modernity and       
 development.                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                       
 The 20th century brought fluorescent lamps, more efficient and long-lasting. LED technology emerged recently,         
 offering unprecedented efficiency and lifespan while reducing energy consumption and environmental impact.            
                                                                                                                       
 From animal fat to LEDs, lamp evolution enabled economic expansion, improved quality of life, and extended human      
 activity into darkness. Modern lighting comprises complex systems-streetlights, task lighting, ambient                
 illumination-that structure modern life. Simple lamps remain civilization's fundamental tool for conquering darkness  
 and extending human potential.
